questions.question: Why does a convex lens bend parallel rays to a focus? Describe the refraction at its two surfaces.
questions.solution: Each surface is a curved refracting boundary: at the first surface rays bend toward the normal (entering glass), at the second away from it (exiting) — and because the surfaces are curved, both bends push the ray toward the axis. The cumulative effect converges parallel rays at F. A lens is two prisms base-to-base in effect.

questions.question: An object is 40 cm from a convex lens of f = 15 cm. Set up 1/v − 1/u = 1/f with correct signs and interpret.
questions.solution: u = −40 cm (object side), f = +15 cm (convex). 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/15 − 1/40 = (8−3)/120 = 5/120 → v = +24 cm. Positive v: image on the OPPOSITE side — real, inverted, magnified m = v/u = −0.6 (diminished). The lens formula's sign convention differs from the mirror's; keeping u negative and f positive for convex is the discipline.

questions.concept: Power of a lens and combinations
questions.question: Define lens power, explain why it is measured in dioptres, and find the power of two thin lenses in contact (+4 D and −2.5 D).
questions.solution: P = 1/f (metres) in dioptres — power adds linearly for thin lenses in contact, which is convenient for prescribing and combining. P = 4 − 2.5 = +1.5 D → f = 1/1.5 ≈ 0.67 m. The additive property is why opticians simply add prescription powers.

questions.question: A magnifying glass gives m = +3. What does the positive sign tell you, and why must the object be inside the focal length?
questions.solution: Positive m means the image is ERECT and VIRTUAL (on the same side as the object) — needed for comfortable viewing. Inside f, refracted rays diverge and only their extensions meet — a magnified virtual image. Beyond f the image becomes real and inverted, useless for reading.

questions.question: Why does a simple lens give coloured fringes at the edges of an image, and how is it corrected?
questions.solution: Dispersion: the lens's refractive index is higher for violet than red, so violet focuses CLOSER to the lens — different focal lengths per colour (chromatic aberration). Correction: an ACHROMATIC DOUBLE — a convex crown-glass lens cemented to a concave flint-glass lens whose opposite dispersion cancels the colour spread while keeping net convergence.
